title: The bill that grew with the tool list
scenario:
You are a finance partner at an online retailer. The customer-service team built an AI assistant that connects to the order system through a set of tools. Usage is rising, and the head of service asks why the bill is higher than the demo suggested.

The engineer sent a cost sheet. The prices are round example numbers, not a vendor's real prices. Use the exhibit to advise.
exhibit:
Monthly cost sheet (made-up example numbers)

Workload: 60,000 requests a month
Per request:
  tool definitions   6,000 tokens (same text every time)
  customer question    500 tokens
  assistant answer     300 tokens

Example prices per million tokens:
  input $1 | cache read $0.10 | output $5

Monthly model cost:
  tool definitions  360M tokens  $360
  questions          30M tokens   $30
  answers            18M tokens   $90
  total                          $480

Not on the sheet: engineer time.
Notes:
  - The team edits tool descriptions about once a week.
  - A separate nightly job summarises 20,000 closed tickets. Nobody reads the summaries before 8 am.

questions.prompt: Which line in the sheet explains most of the bill?

options.text: The assistant's answers, because output tokens cost more than input tokens.
options.explanation: Answers cost $90 of $480. Output tokens are pricier, but there are far fewer of them.

options.text: The customer questions, because they are different every time and cannot be cached.
options.explanation: Questions cost only $30 a month in the sheet.

options.text: The tool definitions: $360 of $480, sent again with every request.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's pricing page counts the tools parameter as input tokens, and OpenAI says function definitions are billed as input tokens. They are paid for on every request.

options.text: Nothing in particular; the cost is spread evenly.
options.explanation: The sheet shows one line at 75% of the total.

questions.prompt: Suppose the definitions were read from cache at the example cache-read price, and the other lines stay the same. Ignore cache writes. About what would the monthly model cost be?

options.text: About $480, because caching does not change the price.
options.explanation: Both vendors list a lower price for cached input, so the sum changes.

options.text: About $156: $36 for definitions, plus $30 and $90.
options.explanation: Right. 360M tokens at $0.10 per million is $36. Add $30 for questions and $90 for answers.

options.text: About $48, which is 10% of the whole $480.
options.explanation: The cache price applies only to the repeated definitions. Questions and answers stay at full price.

options.text: About $36, because only the definitions are billed.
options.explanation: Questions and answers are still billed: $30 and $90.

questions.prompt: The team edits tool descriptions every week. What does that mean for caching?

options.text: Nothing; the cache ignores changes to tool text, so weekly edits cost no extra and need no planning.
options.explanation: Both vendors say the opposite. Changing tool definitions breaks the cached start of the prompt.

options.text: Only the edited tool is re-processed; the other tools stay cached and keep all of their savings.
options.explanation: Anthropic's caching page says modifying tool definitions invalidates the entire cache. OpenAI's guide says reuse needs the full prefix to match.

options.text: Tools can't be cached at all, so caching is not an option for an assistant that uses many tools.
options.explanation: Anthropic lists tool definitions as cacheable content, and OpenAI says tool definitions are part of the cached prefix.

options.text: Each edit breaks the cached prefix, so requests pay full price again; batch edits into rare releases.
options.explanation: Right. Both vendors say a change invalidates the cached prefix. Fewer, planned changes keep the savings.

questions.prompt: How should the nightly summary job for 20,000 closed tickets run?

options.text: As live requests, because the Batch API costs more than the live API.
options.explanation: Both vendors list a 50% discount for batch, not a higher price.

options.text: Through a Batch API, because nobody needs the results before 8 am.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic lists 50% off and says most batches finish in under an hour. OpenAI lists 50% off with results within 24 hours.

options.text: Through the live chat path, so the cache covers it for free.
options.explanation: A cache read is cheaper than full input, but it is not free, and the job pays for it at live prices.

options.text: Move the live customer chat to a Batch API too, to get the discount.
options.explanation: A customer waiting for an answer can't wait for asynchronous results.

questions.prompt: The sheet leaves out engineer time. Which addition makes the comparison with a bought tool fairer? (This checklist is our own framework.)

options.text: Nothing: once built, an integration needs no more work from engineers at all.
options.explanation: Vendors retire models and change tools, so the integration needs updates over time.

options.text: Build time now, plus yearly time to update tools, prompts and tests, for both.
options.explanation: Right. Model usage is only part of the cost. Compare build, run, maintain and review costs of both options over several years.

options.text: Only the licence fee of the bought tool, since the build is already paid for by the team.
options.explanation: That counts one side's extra costs and ignores the other side's maintenance.

options.text: The price of the most expensive model, as a safety margin on the budget.
options.explanation: A margin is not a cost line. It hides which parts of the bill you can reduce.
